explanation: Materialize the entire inorder traversal recursively, then return entry k-1. A strict BST produces increasing inorder values, making that entry the kth smallest; this implementation does not stop traversal early.
timeComplexity: O(n squared) worst-case time: recursive inorder concatenation copies subtree values repeatedly along a skew tree; the final comparison or indexed lookup adds at most O(n).
spaceComplexity: O(n+h) live auxiliary values and recursion frames for n nodes and height h. Completed sibling results and partial inorder arrays together hold O(n) values; cumulative allocation/copying can be quadratic.
attribution: Original repository-authored Blind75 Java algorithm, promoted from the validated correct fixtures. Collection membership follows Crackr; no external solution service is used.
correctness: Recursive inorder concatenation places all left descendants before the root and all right descendants after it. Under the strict BST promise this is a sorted list of every key exactly once. Since k is 1-based and valid, entry k-1 is precisely the requested value.
walkthrough: For [10,4,16,2,7,13,19], build the complete inorder array [2,4,7,10,13,16,19]. With k=4, access index 3 and return 10; nodes after 10 were also traversed.
edgeCases: k is 1-based and within the node count.
A singleton BST with k=1 returns its only value.
Even k=1 builds the full inorder array in this implementation.
